findings.title: NFL trade rule lets a player picked earlier in the same turn be traded for himself, wasting the Trade booster and the second Double pick
findings.scenario: Classic or blind football draft, holding Double Pick and Trade. Land on SF-1980, arm Double and place Joe Montana at QB (picksLeft 1, youDone false). Then tap Trade: tapBooster disarms Double and arms Trade. whyUnavailable(s, Montana) now returns null instead of 'dup', because eligibleSlots = ['QB'] and he is already held at QB. The drawer shows the same Montana row as available, not 'ALREADY ON YOUR TEAM'. Tapping him and then QB dispatches place, which puts the identical player back in the same slot. boostersUsed gains 'trade', so the Draft.tsx effect charges a 70-coin Trade from inventory; the turn ends with picksLeft 0, so the second Double pick is lost; and the toast says 'Traded Joe Montana for Joe Montana.' I reproduced this with the reducer: at 96d5c0c whyUnavailable returns 'dup', at bf23350 it returns null. The same happens for any QB, a DEF, or a back or receiver whose FLEX is empty. No one is ever held twice (I checked that slot ∈ eligibleSlots ⊆ held always replaces the held copy, that pos is the same for every pid in the data, and that a primed version keeps the base id and pos). This no-op is the only regression I found in the rule.
findings.fix: Allow the exception only when the candidate is a different listing of the same person: `const held = SLOTS.filter((k) => s.lineup[k]?.pid === p.pid); const sameListing = held.some((k) => s.lineup[k]!.id === p.id); if (held.length && (sameListing || !(NFL && s.armed === 'trade' && eligibleSlots(s, p).every((k) => held.includes(k))))) return 'dup';`. Add a test: after a Double first pick plus arming Trade, the just-picked player is 'dup'.

findings.title: Weekly-roster 'active' games count game-day inactives and bye weeks, so games are inflated past what a season allows
findings.scenario: active_games() counts every REG row with status == 'ACT'. Before 2020 the weekly-roster files can't support that. In 2002-2015 each team has 17 weekly rows for a 16-game season (the bye week is listed as ACT/A01), and game-day inactives are still status ACT, marked only by status_description_abbr I01/I02. In 2016-2018 ACT also covers inactives. Examples: Andre Johnson 2011 HOU has 17 ACT rows but 8 A01 rows and 7 real games; Andre Johnson 2012 has 17 rows for 16 games. Against PFR's G on one-team seasons, ACT is too high in 85-90% of 2002-2015 seasons and about 47% of 2016-2018 seasons; it is 95% exact only by 2021. The build uses max(stat games, active) for every non-QB row that doesn't get the PFR row: traded seasons 2002-2021, unmatched names, and all Texans (see the HOU finding). Results in the committed nfl.json: 35 lines have more games than their seasons allow (the previous json had 0). Chris Wells ARI-2000 shows 17 g in 2009. Benjamin Watson NE-2000 shows 86 g for 2004-09 (true 71), val 12.54 vs 13.69. Brandon Lloyd DEN-2010 shows 22 g (true 20), 17.24 vs 18.94. Kelvin Benjamin 2017 shows CAR 8 + BUF 9 = 17 in a 16-game season. Percy Harvin NYJ-2010 shows 10 g (true 8). Per-game stats and values come out too low. This disproves the docstring's 'For backs, receivers and tight ends it matches PFR's games played'.
findings.fix: Count only weeks the team played (join (season, week, team) to games.csv REG games) and skip rows whose status_description_abbr starts with 'I'. Only trust the count from 2020 on (or wherever it matches PFR's G). For traded seasons 2002-2021, split the PFR 2TM row's G across the stints instead: cap each stint at its team-weeks and make the sum equal PFR's G. Or fall back to stat-games before 2020.

findings.title: pfr_franchise maps HOU to TEN for every season and leaves LVR unmapped, so the PFR one-team fix never applies to the Texans (2002-21) or the 2020-21 Raiders
findings.scenario: pfr_franchise('HOU', y) returns 'TEN' for all y. That was correct for the 1970-98 Oilers, but pfr_rows now reads 1999-2021, and from 2002 'HOU' in the PFR tables means the Texans. 'LVR' (2020-21) is not mapped either, so it never equals 'LV'. In verse_rows, p['fr'] == a['fr'] then fails for 332 Texans player-seasons and 35 Raiders ones, so they keep nflverse games. Non-QBs fall through to the inflated active count. Results in the committed json: Andre Johnson HOU-2000 has 119 g in 7 seasons (max 112, PFR 102), val 19.65 -> 16.22 (Epic to Rare); with the mapping fixed it is 19.7. Andre Johnson HOU-2010 has 85 g in 5 seasons (PFR 67), 18.36 -> 14.29 (fixed: 18.85). Arian Foster HOU-2010 has 80 g (PFR 70), 21.65 Legendary -> 18.89 Epic (fixed: 21.92). DeAndre Hopkins HOU-2010 has 115 g in 7 seasons. Ron Dayne, Owen Daniels, Domanick Williams and Cecil Shorts all drop 1.5-3.7. The Texans' playoff-opponent lines (2011, 2012, 2015, 2016, 2018, 2019) use the same inflated games. The Texans' rows are also labelled TEN in settle_ids, so they chain against the Titans' namesakes.
findings.fix: In pfr_franchise, return 'TEN' for 'HOU' only when season <= 1998 and 'HOU' after; map 'LVR' to 'LV'. Then assert that every non-xTM PFR row from 1999-2021 maps to a code in FRANCHISES. A scratch rebuild with this change brings the Texans' lines back to PFR's games.

findings.title: A Prime can still point to a line of equal value: the check compares round(val,2), but the app compares sums of separately rounded parts
findings.scenario: pr_ref is set when round(pr[0],2) > round(a['val'],2) + 0.01. The json stores val split into r_pass/r_rush/r_recv, each rounded on its own, and the app's val is their sum. In the committed json, Tim Hightower ARI-2000 (parts 0, 7.77, 3.44 = 11.209999...) has prime ARI-2010 (0, 9.56, 1.65 = 11.21). Both show 11.21, and primeVersion accepts it only by float noise (best.val > p.val by about 1e-15), so the player is offered a Prime 'upgrade' worth nothing. This breaks the commit's claim that every Prime points to a better line.
findings.fix: Rebuild both lines' stored parts (round(val*share_i, 2)) and compare those sums, requiring the prime's sum to exceed the line's by at least 0.01. Or compute pr_ref after the rounded parts are built.

findings.title: The room-mismatch SWITCH button changes sport without waiting for the finished match's last resends
findings.scenario: The commit says switching sport now waits for a just-finished match's last resends. Only App.goSport (the Home sport switch) does that, by waiting until lingerUntil. The SWITCH TO NFL/NBA button in Search's friend-room mismatch notice calls switchSport(mm.sport, room!.code) directly, and that reloads the page at once. Concrete path: finish a head-to-head match (finish() calls endMatch(false, 30000), so the final state is re-sent every 2.5 s for 30 s). Tap Play again, which runs startRun('1v1') and opens Search. Tap PLAY A FRIEND and join a code whose host is on the other sport; the mismatch notice appears within about 2 s. Tap SWITCH about 10-15 s after the match ended. The page reloads, and the last 15-20 s of resends are cut, which is exactly what goSport now prevents. Impact is small: close() already stored the final state, and the other phone looks it up when it hears nothing for a while.
findings.fix: Make App the single place that switches sport and have it respect lingerUntil. For example, give Search an onSwitch(to, room) prop that App wires to a goSport variant taking a room. That variant would compute wait = max(420, lingerUntil.current - Date.now()), show the sportfade overlay (with the 'Sending your match's last picks first…' line when wait > 1000), call saveProfile, then call switchSport(to, room) after the wait. It must skip the screen === 'tab' guard, since this switch happens from the search screen.

findings.title: Perfect-season reveal still clips START THE PLAYOFFS on the shortest compact screens (NFL below ~565 frame px of content, NBA below ~550)
findings.scenario: I rendered Reveal in Chromium through the dev server with a 17-0 (or 82-0) season and reducedMotion, so the final layout shows at once. The new compact rules (sched 28px, smaller .unbeaten, no qualify line) fit SE-class phones: 375x553 has 9.7px to spare, 375x548 has 4.7px. They do not fit the 540 frame-px floor the frame is designed for (MIN_CONTENT in stage.tsx). The NFL button sticks out past the stage bottom, which has overflow: hidden, and is clipped by 25 frame px at 390x540 (half of the button text is cut), 20 at 545, 15 at 550, 10 at 555 and 5 at 560. Two real cases: an Android 360x640 phone with on-screen nav buttons in Chrome (viewport about 360x512) loses 9.5 screen px, and a 320x460 iPhone SE (1st gen) in Safari loses 3.6px. The NBA reveal is clipped by 9px at 540 and 4px at 545. The main cause is the three result pills, which wrap onto two rows in compact. The commit message says 'A perfect season's reveal fits small phones'.
findings.fix: Win back about 25 frame px in compact while the reveal is done and unbeaten. For example: hide the 'Final record' eyebrow (.fit-compact .reveal .board.gold ~ .gameno { display: none }), shrink .fit-compact .reveal .pill (padding 5px 8px, font-size 11px) so the three pills fit on one row, or cut .fit-compact .verdict gap to 6px. Add a 390x540 perfect-reveal case for both sports to the device fit check.

findings.title: YARDS sort adds yards the row never shows, so football lists still sort against the highlighted columns
findings.scenario: hotFor now lights every yards column a row shows: a QB's PASS and RUSH, an RB's RUSH and YDS, a WR or TE's YDS and RUSH. But sortValue('yds') still adds passYds + rushYds + recYds, so a back's or receiver's thrown-pass yards and a QB's receiving yards count without being shown. Example: the 2020s Patriots sorted by YARDS put Julian Edelman (lit YDS 53 + RUSH 4 = 56; plus 6.3 hidden passing yards a game) directly above Stefon Diggs (lit YDS 60 + RUSH 0). The 1970s Chargers put Mike Montgomery (lit RUSH 21 + YDS 33 = 53; plus 7.3 hidden passing) above Lydell Mitchell (37 + 24 = 60). The 1980s Patriots put Andy Johnson (lit 22) above Don Hasselbeck (28) and Stephen Starring (26). Across all 183 football lists I found 4 inversions of 3 yards or more, plus many 1-2 yard ones. This breaks the commit's claim that 'football sorts follow the highlighted columns'.
findings.fix: Sum only the columns the row shows, e.g. `if (key === 'yds') return statCols(p).filter((c) => c.key.endsWith('Yds')).reduce((a, c) => a + c.value, 0);`. Equivalently, by position: QB passYds+rushYds, RB rushYds+recYds, others recYds+rushYds.

findings.title: Football first-launch screen still pre-fills a basketball-slang name
findings.scenario: Welcome (src/ui/Welcome.tsx:10) seeds the name field with useState(randomName), and the dice button also uses randomName. Its word lists are basketball-only and ignore NFL: Splash, Swish, Dunk, Fadeaway, Hoop, Buzzer, Rim, Glass, Downtown, Posterize, Alley, Crossover, Baseline, Paint, Sixth, Mamba. A first launch at ?sport=nfl therefore opens on a name like 'SwishMamba42' or 'HoopLegend17', right under the new 'Draft six players from random NFL teams' line. The commit message says 'the first-launch screen speaks football'.
findings.fix: Give football its own FIRST list (e.g. Blitz, Gridiron, Endzone, Hailmary, Redzone, Shotgun, Pylon, Audible, Pocket, Fourth) and choose the list with NFL from engine/sport, or use sport-neutral words for both.

findings.title: Shared lastName still cuts some compound surnames to their last word (not a regression)
findings.scenario: I ran lastName over all 4,553 NBA and 3,054 NFL player names plus the playoff opponents. Nothing renders worse than before: every changed result is right (Van Exel, Van Horn, Van Lier, Van Arsdale, Del Negro, Da Silva, De Colo, Vander Velden, van Eeghen, Van Heusen, St. Brown), and 'Jr.'/'III' handling and single-word names like Nenê are fine. Some names were already wrong in the old share.ts, common.tsx and cardName and still are. 'Antwaan Randle El' becomes 'El' on his lineup card, in leaderboard lines, in history, in share text and in the Scout one-liner (he is also a playoff opponent). 'Luc Mbah a Moute' becomes 'Moute', 'George Bon Salle' becomes 'Salle', 'Jan van Breda Kolff' becomes 'Kolff' and 'Metta World Peace' becomes 'Peace'. The new doc comment describes the rule as 'the last name with its St. or Van'.
findings.fix: Add a small override map for compound surnames the particle rule can't catch (Randle El, Mbah a Moute, Bon Salle, van Breda Kolff, World Peace), or have the data build emit a short-name field for those players and prefer it in lastName.

The finding is real. I tried to refute it and could not.

1. Raw data (.cache/nfl/rw/2011.csv, 2012.csv). Andre Johnson HOU (listed as HST) has 17 REG rows in 2011, weeks 1-17, every one with status ACT. Nine of them have status_description_abbr I01, meaning game-day inactive. Only 8 are A01, which is his 7 real games plus the bye week. In 2012 he has 17 REG rows, all ACT/A01, for a 16-game season. active_games() (scripts/nfl_sources.py:292-301) counts every REG + ACT row, so it returns 17 in both years.

2. Ran the actual code. I imported the repo's nfl_sources and called verse_rows, season_rosters, active_games, pfr_rows and team_games (scripts are in the scratchpad at review2/). I compared active counts with PFR G for one-team RB/WR/TE seasons where the ids match. Active is higher than PFR G in 94-99% of seasons in each year from 2002 to 2015, 49-56% in 2016-2018, 22% in 2019, 17% in 2020 and 6% in 2021. That is worse than the reviewer said. So the docstring's claim that it "matches PFR's games played" is false before about 2020.

3. Where the fallback fires. verse_rows line 363 does a["g"] = max(stat_g, active) for every non-QB row that doesn't take the PFR row. Three groups land there:
   - All Texans 2002-2021, because pfr_franchise maps HOU to TEN, so the team check p["fr"] == a["fr"] fails.
   - Traded seasons.
   - Names the register can't match. PFR's "Ben Watson" and "Beanie Wells" get stand-in pfr: ids, so Benjamin Watson and Chris Wells fall back too.

   Among substantive RB/WR/TE rows from 2002-2021, 125 HOU rows, 60 traded rows and 59 others take their games from the active count. Andre Johnson's 2011 HOU row comes out at g=17; the truth is 7. For traded seasons, the stint totals beat PFR's combined G in 12 of 54 cases. Examples: Percy Harvin 2014 SEA 6 + NYJ 10 = 16 against a combined G of 13; Vernon Davis 2015 8 + 9 = 17 against 15; Roy Williams 2008 6 + 11 = 17 against 15.

4. Committed src/data/nfl.json. I flagged any line whose games exceed its seasons × 16 (17 from 2021). The new json has exactly 35 such lines; the json at 96d5c0c has 0. Examples:
   - Andre Johnson HOU-2000: 119 g over 7 seasons, where 112 is the most possible and 102 is the truth. The old json had 101. His receiving yards per game drop from 78.7 to 66.8, and his receiving rating from 19.57 to 16.15.
   - Benjamin Watson NE-2000: 86 g; PFR says 71, the old json said 65.
   - Chris Wells ARI-2009: 17 g in a 16-game season.
   - DeAndre Hopkins HOU-2010: 115 g over 7 seasons. His receiving rating drops from 17.17 to 16.37, and he now carries a prime pointer to ARI-2020.

So this is a regression the commit introduced, and it contradicts what the commit says it does. Per-game stats and values for every Texans line from 2002-2021, plus traded and unmatched players, come out too low.

Severity: medium is fair. The HOU-to-TEN mapping is a separate finding that makes this one bigger; even with it fixed, traded and unmatched seasons from 2002-2018 are still inflated.

Fix:
- In active_games, count only weeks the team actually played: join (season, week, team) to the REG games in games.csv.
- Skip rows whose status_description_abbr starts with 'I'.
- Trust the count only from about 2020 on.
- For traded seasons from 2002-2021, split the PFR 2TM row's G across the stints, capping each stint at its team's games, so the stints add up to PFR's G.
- Otherwise, fall back to stat games before 2020.

The lines are scripts/nfl_sources.py:299 (the count) and :363 (the max).

I reproduced it, and it is real but low severity: it affects exactly one line in the committed data.

What I checked:
1. I scanned all 2441 Prime references in the committed src/data/nfl.json (`git show bf23350:src/data/nfl.json`). For each one I computed the value the app uses, which is lineValue: r_pass + r_rush + r_recv + r_def, all weights 1 (src/engine/rating.ts:73, src/engine/data.ts:107). No Prime has a gain of zero or less. Exactly one has a gain below 0.0095: Tim Hightower ARI-2000 has parts [0, 7.77, 3.44, 0], which sum to 11.209999999999999. His prime ARI-2010 has [0, 9.56, 1.65, 0], which sum to 11.21. The gain is 1.78e-15. primeVersion (src/engine/data.ts:146, `best.val <= p.val` returns null) accepts it only because of float noise. The new test in src/engine/nfl.test.ts ("every Prime points to ... a better line") passes for the same reason.
2. I rebuilt the data from .cache/nfl with an unmodified copy of the bf23350 scripts in the scratch dir; the output is byte-identical to the committed json. I added a debug dump to get the Python values. ARI-2000 val is 11.2006084, ARI-2010 val (the prime) is 11.2118652, and the true difference is 0.011. The guard at scripts/build_nfl_data.py:317 is `round(pr[0],2) > round(a['val'],2) + 0.01`, which here is 11.21 > 11.20 + 0.01. In Python, 11.20 + 0.01 = 11.209999999999999, so the guard passes by float noise as well. In exact arithmetic it would be false and the Prime would have been dropped. So there are two causes: the guard has no tolerance for float error, and it compares the unrounded val while the app compares sums of separately rounded parts.
3. Effect in the UI (src/ui/Draft.tsx:806-822 and pickRow at 619-633): with Prime armed in the ARI-2000 cell, Hightower shows as primeable with the tag 'PRIME: ARI 2010s'. Spending the booster (one per draft, 100 coins) leaves his value unchanged at 11.21 and only moves about 1.79 from receiving to rushing. The hint banner needs a gain of at least 5, so it never suggests him.

This breaks the commit's claim that "every Prime points to a listed, better line" for this one case. The impact is narrow: one line out of about 5500, a mid-value back, and the player sees the primed stats before tapping.

Fix: in build_nfl_data.py, build each line's stored parts first (round(val*share_i, 2)) and set pr_ref only when the prime's stored-part sum minus this line's stored-part sum is at least 0.01 minus a small epsilon (e.g. 1e-9). Alternatively, compare `round(pr[0] - a['val'], 2) >= 0.02`, or use a margin that does not land exactly on a rounding step. In primeVersion, a check like `best.val - p.val < 0.005` would make the app robust to float noise too.

The code path exists, but it is not a regression, and losing those resends has a negligible effect. What I checked:

(1) It is not a regression. At 96d5c0c the Search mismatch button already called switchSport(mismatch.sport, room!.code) straight away (git show 96d5c0c:src/ui/Search.tsx, line 206). bf23350 only renamed mismatch to mm in that line. The commit added the lingerUntil wait to App.goSport, the Home sport switcher. The commit line "Switching sport waits for a just-finished match's last resends" fairly describes that switcher.

(2) The path is reachable. For a 1v1 match, finish() runs at draft completion and calls endMatch(false, 30000). Results then offers onAgain, which calls startRun('1v1') and opens Search. From there, PLAY A FRIEND plus a code whose host is on the other sport shows the mismatch notice through the 2 s lobby announce, and SWITCH reloads at once. So a reload inside the 30 s linger window can happen.

(3) The effect is negligible. MatchConn.close(false, 30000) in src/net/match.ts calls persist() synchronously before it starts the 2.5 s resend interval. That stores the final state as a KIND_APP event with a 1-day expiry. The final pick also went out live at once through update() -> send() when it was made. By the 10-15 s mark in the scenario, the final state has gone out live about 5-7 times and has been stored. The resends only matter when the finishing player made the round's last pick and the other phone missed every one of those sends. In that case the other phone recovers on its own:
- MatchConn.start's timer calls lookup() after 12 s of silence, before gone() turns true at 20 s and before the Draft's AI takeover. lookup() then take()s the stored final picks.
- onVisible also calls lookup() when that phone comes back from the background.
So the other phone still gets the real final picks and the correct result. Cutting the remaining resends changes nothing in practice; the finding itself admits the impact is small.

(4) Nothing else is lost by the instant reload. Profile state, including activeMatch: null from finish and the queued leaderboard entries, is already saved by useEffect(() => saveProfile(profile), [profile]) in App.tsx line 112. So the reload does not record a false forfeit or drop entries.

This is a narrow, pre-existing gap in an extra safety layer, with a working fallback behind it. It is not a defect with a wrong output.

NFL 17-0 is clipped by 25 frame px at 390x540, 15 at 550 and 5 at 560, and fits at 570. 375x553 and 375x548 have 9.7 and 4.7 screen px to spare. 360x512 is clipped by 9.5 screen px and 320x460 by 3.6. NBA 82-0 is clipped by 9 at 540 and 4 at 545, and fits at 550 and on every real-device size. The three pills wrap onto two rows.

2. Not a regression. The parent is much worse at the same sizes:
   - 390x540: 73 frame px clipped (now 25).
   - 360x512: 53.9 screen px (now 9.5).
   - 320x460: 43 (now 3.6).
   - 375x553: 36.4 (now fits).
   - NBA at 540: 39 (now 9).

3. On the real devices named, only the button's bottom edge is cut. Screenshots at 320x460 and 360x512 show the label fully readable and the button fully visible and tappable. A 3.6px trim on the SE 1st gen is invisible in practice. The 9.5px case only happens on old 16:9 360x640 Android phones in Chrome with 3-button nav, and even there the label is intact.

4. The bad case, with the label half cut, needs content at the 540 floor, which means a viewport aspect ratio below about 1.385. That is not a normal portrait phone with standard browser chrome. At that floor the NFL reveal is clipped whatever the record: 14-3 and 5-12 are both clipped by 9 frame px at bf23350 (27 at the parent). So this is an old shortfall of the reveal at the floor, not something on the perfect-season path the commit claimed to fix, and the commit made it smaller.

5. The commit's claim that a perfect season's reveal fits small phones holds for the phones the project targets. The smallest phone in the project's device fit check is se-safari at 375x548, and the reveal fits there with 4.7px to spare, as it does at 375x553, the SE home-screen app, the mini and larger.
